source.title: European Union Serious and Organised Crime Threat Assessment – The changing DNA of serious and organised crime (EU-SOCTA 2025)

summary: Europol's EU-SOCTA 2025 assesses the EU organised-crime landscape as destabilising, nurtured online, and accelerated by AI. Financial-crime relevant strands: money laundering evolving via crypto mixing services, chain-hopping and DeFi as a 'digital cloak'; pervasive abuse of shell/buffer companies to launder proceeds and commit VAT/customs fraud; digitalising corruption with corruption brokers and crypto/fintech-paid bribes; and a dedicated sanctions-evasion section on trade-based evasion of EU sanctions on Russia via front companies, falsified documentation and transhipment through the Eurasian Economic Union/Caucasus, increasingly aided by crypto. A central theme is criminal networks acting as proxies for state-aligned hybrid threat actors (sabotage, cyber-attacks, disinformation, laundering) via a persistent, cumulative 'woodpecker' pattern. The report also covers many physical crime areas (drugs, firearms, migrant smuggling, THB, cyber-attacks, fraud, CSAM, property/environmental crime) summarised but not separately typology-tagged, as outside the Knowledge Centre's financial-crime-analytics scope.

citations.quote: In early 2024, Dutch authorities arrested three individuals for allegedly exporting military-grade goods to Russia, in violation of European Union sanctions.
Trade-based sanctions evasion relies heavily on a crime-as-a-service model combined with infiltration into legitimate businesses to handle the supply chain.
These illicit exports were allegedly facilitated through front companies and falsified documentation to circumvent trade restrictions.
Legal businesses are infiltrated, and front companies are set up in retail, import-export, transport, or the financial sector for the procurement and shipment of goods or assets.

It is likely that criminal networks increasingly leverage tools such as encrypted communications, anonymised financial transactions, cryptocurrencies and blockchain technologies, and cyber-enabled trade-based money laundering.
For example, front or shell companies may be used to facilitate the movement of illicit or stolen goods or to enable money laundering activities.
Criminals make use of limited liability companies, individual entrepreneurs, and shell companies, which they quickly establish and dissolve.
Shell or buffer companies, whether infiltrated or set-up, facilitate the exploitation of cross-border VAT systems and VAT refund processes.

typologies.label: Cryptocurrency Layering via Mixing Services, Chain-Hopping and DeFi

citations.quote: Deposited funds would be turned into “chips” (small tokens with equivalent value), which were then mixed together - thereby anonymising all trails to where the initial funds originated.
Chain hopping, for example, involves the switching between different cryptocurrencies to obscure the origin of funds.
the elevated role of corruption brokers.
Bribes are transferred by criminally exploiting cryptocurrencies or fintech.

typologies.label: Hybrid Threat Actor Use of Criminal Networks as Proxies (Woodpecker Modus Operandi)

citations.quote: It is also progressively driven by hybrid threats, directed externally, that encompass a broad range of criminal activities and tactics operated via criminal proxies.

Much like a woodpecker weakens a tree over time through repeated strikes, hybrid threat actors engage in ongoing, seemingly minor actions that collectively erode stability, security, and trust in institutions.

actors.name: Criminal networks
actors.role: Primary perpetrators across all crime areas described in the report; increasingly act as proxies for hybrid threat actors while retaining financial motivation

citations.quote: While criminal networks are in it for the financial profits, their activities contribute to the political goals of the hybrid threat actor they support.

actors.name: Hybrid threat actors
actors.role: State or state-aligned actors who cooperate with and outsource criminal activity (sabotage, disinformation, cyber-attacks, money laundering) to criminal networks for deniability and geopolitical gain

citations.quote: Some states provide safe havens for criminals in exchange for their services, allowing them to operate freely without fear of prosecution.

actors.name: Professional money launderers / money brokers
actors.role: Specialised launderers who operate parallel, underground financial systems outside regulated frameworks, offering large-scale unregulated financial services to multiple criminal networks

citations.quote: Some high-level money brokers occupy pivotal positions within criminal networks, offering extensive, unregulated financial services to multiple criminal networks.

actors.name: Corruption brokers
actors.role: Intermediaries emerging under the crime-as-a-service model to facilitate corrupt access to public and private sector systems

citations.quote: corruption has adapted to the broader trends toward digitalisation and a crime-as-a-service model, with several threats becoming increasingly visible: ... the elevated role of corruption brokers.

actors.name: ChipMixer
actors.role: Unlicensed cryptocurrency mixing service used to launder illicit crypto assets by tokenising and mixing deposits

citations.quote: ChipMixer, an unlicensed cryptocurrency mixer, was taken down in March 2023, for its alleged involvement in money laundering activities.

actors.name: Front companies (sanctions-evasion supply chains)
actors.role: Entities set up or infiltrated in retail, import-export, transport and financial sectors to procure and ship sanctioned goods while concealing the real party in interest

citations.quote: Legal businesses are infiltrated, and front companies are set up in retail, import-export, transport, or the financial sector for the procurement and shipment of goods or assets.

indicators.description: Use of front companies and falsified export documentation to disguise military-grade or sanctioned goods shipped to sanctioned destinations

citations.quote: These illicit exports were allegedly facilitated through front companies and falsified documentation to circumvent trade restrictions.

indicators.description: Infiltration of legitimate businesses and establishment of front companies across retail, import-export, transport and financial sectors to run sanctions-evasion supply chains

citations.quote: Legal businesses are infiltrated, and front companies are set up in retail, import-export, transport, or the financial sector for the procurement and shipment of goods or assets.

indicators.description: Chain-hopping between cryptocurrencies, including conversion into lesser-known coins or privacy coins such as Monero, to obscure the origin of funds

citations.quote: These transactions are difficult to trace when well-known coins are exchanged into less known ones or privacy coins like Monero, enhancing anonymity.

indicators.description: Deposits processed through an unlicensed cryptocurrency mixing service that converts funds into interchangeable tokens before redistribution, severing the audit trail back to source

citations.quote: Deposited funds would be turned into “chips” (small tokens with equivalent value), which were then mixed together - thereby anonymising all trails to where the initial funds originated.

indicators.description: Use of shell or buffer companies with no genuine commercial substance, quickly established and dissolved, to exploit cross-border VAT refund and customs processes

citations.quote: Shell or buffer companies, whether infiltrated or set-up, facilitate the exploitation of cross-border VAT systems and VAT refund processes.

indicators.description: Recruitment and communication with corrupt insiders conducted online, with bribes settled via cryptocurrency or fintech channels

citations.quote: Recruitment of, and communication with corruptees takes place online. Bribes are transferred by criminally exploiting cryptocurrencies or fintech.

indicators.description: Criminal networks executing persistent, cumulative, seemingly minor disruptive incidents (sabotage, arson, intimidation) on behalf of external hybrid threat actors rather than a single major attack

citations.quote: Such incidents may be part of a larger strategic objective of destabilisation, involving persistent, targeted, and cumulative disruptions rather than a single, overwhelming attack.

indicators.description: Transhipment of sanctioned strategic goods routed via Eurasian Economic Union and Caucasus countries en route to Russia and Belarus

citations.quote: Countries from the Eurasian Economic Union and the Caucasus play a central role in transhipment.

extraction_notes: This is a 100-page, EU-wide strategic threat assessment covering nearly the entire organised-crime landscape (cyber-attacks, online fraud, CSAM, human trafficking, migrant smuggling, drug and firearms trafficking, environmental crime, property crime, IP crime, currency counterfeiting, EU-financial-interest fraud). Only the strands with direct financial-crime/Knowledge Centre relevance (sanctions evasion, shell-company/TBML abuse, crypto layering, corruption, and the hybrid-threat/criminal-proxy nexus) were extracted as typologies; the remaining crime areas are reflected only in the summary. Confidence on CMI010 and the corruption-broker emergent typology is comparatively low/medium because each rests on a small number of narrative sentences rather than a developed case study. The 'Hybrid Threat Actor Use of Criminal Networks as Proxies' item is proposed as emergent because no existing KC family/typology captures state-criminal proxy relationships, even though it is arguably the report's central thesis. Jurisdictions listed reflect countries named in the specific passages cited (sanctions case: NL/DE/LV/LT/RU; hybrid threat state-actor context: RU/CN/IR/KP/UA) rather than the full geographic scope of the report.
